subject: math
title: Grade 6 Angles: Classify, Estimate and Measure
seo_title: Grade 6 Angles Worksheets: Classify, Estimate and Measure (Free Math with Answer Key, BC Curriculum)
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 math worksheets on angles for the BC curriculum: classify acute, right, obtuse, straight and reflex angles, estimate with benchmark angles, read both protractor scales and find missing angles on a straight line and around a point. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Estimate first, then read the protractor scale that starts at 0 on your arm.
key_sub: Acute is less than 90°, obtuse is between 90° and 180°, and reflex is between 180° and 360°. Angles on a straight line add up to 180°; angles around a point add up to 360°.
body_html:
Classify angles

An angle is an amount of turn between two arms. We measure it in degrees (°). A full turn is 360°, a straight angle (half a turn) is 180° and a right angle (a quarter turn) is 90°.

NameSize
Acute angleless than 90°
Right angleexactly 90°
Obtuse anglemore than 90°, less than 180°
Straight angleexactly 180°
Reflex anglemore than 180°, less than 360°

Estimate with benchmarks

Compare the angle with angles you know: 45° (half a right angle), 90°, 135°, 180° and 270° (three right angles). Estimate first, then measure. If the measurement is far from your estimate, check it.

Estimate

An angle opens a little wider than a square corner. Estimate it.

It is more than 90° but less than 135°.

Answer: about 110° to 120°

Read a protractor

1. Put the centre of the protractor on the vertex. 2. Line up one arm with 0. 3. Read the scale that starts at 0 on that arm. 4. Check the reading against your estimate.

A protractor only goes to 180°. To find a reflex angle, measure the angle on the other side, then subtract from 360°.

Reflex angle

The gap on the other side of a reflex angle measures 130°. Find the reflex angle.

The two angles make a full turn: 360° − 130° = 230°.

Answer: 230°

Angles on a line and around a point

Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. Angles that go all the way around a point add up to 360°.

Missing angle around a point

Three angles go around a point. Two are 90° and 150°. Find the third.

90° + 150° = 240°. 360° − 240° = 120°.

Answer: 120°

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Reading the wrong scale (140° for a 40° angle)Read the scale that starts at 0 on your arm, then check your estimate
Calling 190° obtuseObtuse is between 90° and 180°. More than 180° is reflex
Thinking long arms make a big angleThe size is the turn between the arms, not their length
Using 180° for angles around a pointAround a point is a full turn: 360°. A straight line is 180°

faq.q: What do Grade 6 students learn about angles in the BC math curriculum?
faq.a: In Grade 6, BC students measure and classify angles as acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex. They estimate with benchmark angles such as 45°, 90° and 180° and use a protractor to measure and draw angles.

faq.q: Why does a protractor have two scales?
faq.a: So you can measure from an arm on either side: the inner scale starts at 0 on the right, and the outer scale starts at 0 on the left. Always read the scale that starts at 0 on your arm, then check the answer against your estimate.

faq.q: How do you measure a reflex angle with a protractor?
faq.a: A protractor only goes to 180°, so measure the angle on the other side of the arms and subtract it from 360°. For example, if the other side is 70°, the reflex angle is 290°.

faq.q: Do angles on a straight line always add up to 180°?
faq.a: Yes. A straight line is half a turn, so the angles on it add up to 180°. Angles that go all the way around a point add up to 360°.

sets.title: Classify angles: acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex

items.q: An angle measures 91°. How do you classify it?
items.e: 91° is more than 90° but less than 180°, so it is obtuse (only just). A right angle is exactly 90°.
An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle: between 90° and 180°. This angle is 160°.

items.q: Classify the marked angle.
items.e: A right angle is exactly 90°, a quarter turn. The small square shows it. Turning the angle does not change its size or its name.

A reflex angle is bigger than a straight angle but smaller than a full turn: between 180° and 360°. Look at the arc: it goes around the outside. This angle is 265°. (The gap between the arms is 95°, but the arc marks the big angle around the outside.)
A straight angle is exactly 180°, half a turn. The two arms make a straight line.

items.q: Which list goes from the smallest angle to the largest?
items.e: Acute is less than 90°, right is 90°, obtuse is between 90° and 180°, straight is 180° and reflex is between 180° and 360°.
A reflex angle is more than 180°: its arc goes around the outside. C is about 250°. A is obtuse, B is acute and D is a right angle.

items.q: How many degrees are in a full turn?
items.e: A full turn is 360°. It is 4 right angles: 4 × 90° = 360°. 180° is a straight angle, only half a turn.

items.q: Classify the marked angle.
items.e: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle: less than 90°. This angle is 70°. Turning the angle does not change its size or its name.

items.q: An angle measures 175°. How do you classify it?
items.e: 175° is more than 90° but less than 180°, so it is obtuse. It is close to a straight angle, but not 180°.

items.q: Hana says an angle of 190° is obtuse because it is bigger than 90°. Is she right?
items.e: Obtuse angles are bigger than 90° but smaller than 180°. 190° is more than 180°, so it is reflex.

A reflex angle is bigger than a straight angle but smaller than a full turn: between 180° and 360°. Look at the arc: it goes around the outside. This angle is 320°. (The gap between the arms is 40°, but the arc marks the big angle around the outside.)

A reflex angle is bigger than a straight angle but smaller than a full turn: between 180° and 360°. Look at the arc: it goes around the outside. This angle is 230°. (The gap between the arms is 130°, but the arc marks the big angle around the outside.)
An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle: between 90° and 180°. This angle is 100°. Turning the angle does not change its size or its name.
A straight angle is exactly 180°, half a turn. The two arms make a straight line. Turning the angle does not change its size or its name.
An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle: between 90° and 180°. This angle is 125°.

items.q: Which list has only reflex angles?
items.e: Reflex angles are more than 180° and less than 360°. 200°, 270° and 345° all fit. 100°, 150° and 175° are obtuse, 180° is straight and 45° is acute.

items.q: An angle measures 89°. How do you classify it?
items.e: 89° is less than 90°, so it is acute (only just). A right angle is exactly 90°.

items.q: Classify the marked angle.
items.e: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle: less than 90°. This angle is 35°.

items.q: An angle measures 185°. How do you classify it?
items.e: 185° is more than 180° but less than 360°, so it is reflex, even though it is close to a straight angle.

items.q: What angle is halfway between a right angle and a straight angle?
items.e: Halfway between 90° and 180° is 135°, because 90° + 45° = 135°. (270° comes from adding 90° + 180°.)
The marked angle is more than a straight angle (180°) but less than three right angles (270°). Halfway between is 225°. (135° is the gap on the other side: 360° − 225° = 135°.)

items.q: Use benchmark angles (45°, 90°, 135°, 180°, 270°). Which is the best estimate for the marked angle?
items.e: The angle looks like a square corner, so it is about 90°. (It is 88°.)

items.q: Which angle is closer to a straight angle: 165° or 200°?

items.e: The arc goes around the outside and is a little more than a straight angle (180°), so it is about 200°. (160° is the gap between the arms, the angle on the other side.)
The angle is about halfway between a right angle (90°) and a straight angle (180°), so it is about 135°.

items.q: Which angle is closest to 45°?
items.e: 45° is half a right angle. B is about half of a square corner. A is nearly a right angle, C is very small and D is obtuse.

items.q: Noah estimates an angle as about 135°. Then he measures it with a protractor and reads 45°. What should he do?
items.e: 45° is far from the estimate of 135°, so Noah probably read the wrong scale. The other scale gives 180° − 45° = 135°, which matches the estimate.
The arc goes around the outside and leaves a gap of about a right angle. 360° − 90° = 270°. (90° is the gap, not the marked angle.)

items.q: An angle is a little smaller than a right angle. Which could it be?
items.e: A right angle is 90°. A little smaller than 90° is about 80°. 100° is a little bigger.
The angle is a bit more than a right angle (90°), but less than 135°. About 120° fits. (60° would be acute.)
270° is three right angles, so the gap between the arms is a right angle. C leaves a square-corner gap. A is about 200°, B is about 300° and D is about 330°.
The gap between the arms is about 45°, half a right angle. The marked angle goes around the outside: 360° − 45° = 315°. (45° is only the gap.)

items.q: An angle is bigger than a straight angle but smaller than three right angles. Which could it be?
items.e: It must be between 180° and 270°. Only 230° fits. 130° and 170° are less than 180°, and 290° is more than 270°.

items.q: Use benchmark angles (45°, 90°, 135°, 180°, 270°). Which is the best estimate for the marked angle?
items.e: The angle is about half of a right angle, so it is about 45°.
The size of an angle is the amount of turn between the arms, not the length of the arms. A opens the widest (about 150°), even though its arms are the shortest.

items.q: An angle is a little bigger than a straight angle. Which could it be?
items.e: A straight angle is 180°. A little bigger is about 190°, a reflex angle. 170° is a little smaller.

items.q: Use benchmark angles (45°, 90°, 135°, 180°, 270°). Which is the best estimate for the marked angle?
items.e: The angle is less than half a right angle (45°). About 30° fits. (150° is what the other scale of a protractor would say.)
The arms almost make a straight line (180°), so the angle is about 170°. (10° is the small gap left to make a straight line, and 190° would be reflex.)

items.q: How many degrees are in three quarters of a full turn?
items.e: A full turn is 360°. One quarter is 90°, so three quarters is 3 × 90° = 270°. (75° comes from mixing up three quarters with 75%.)

items.q: Neither arm is on 0. What is the size of the angle?
items.e: On the inner scale one arm is at 20 and the other is at 95. The angle is the difference: 95° − 20° = 75°. (95° comes from reading only one arm.)

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the left, so read the outer scale. It counts clockwise from 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 100. (The inner scale says 80 there.) The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 100° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the left, so read the outer scale. It counts clockwise from 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 30. (The inner scale says 150 there.) The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 30° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the left, so read the outer scale. It counts clockwise from 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 120. (The inner scale says 60 there.) The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 120° makes sense.

items.q: Neither arm is on 0. What is the size of the angle?
items.e: On the inner scale one arm is at 40 and the other is at 150. The angle is the difference: 150° − 40° = 110°. (150° comes from reading only one arm.)

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the left, so read the outer scale. It counts clockwise from 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 70. (The inner scale says 110 there.) The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 70° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the right, so read the inner scale. It counts counterclockwise from 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 155. The small marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 150 and 160 is 155. The outer scale says 25 there, but it counts from the other side. The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 155° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the right, so read the inner scale. It counts counterclockwise from 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 80. The outer scale says 100 there, but it counts from the other side. The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 80° makes sense.

items.q: Where do you put the centre of the protractor when you measure an angle?
c: at the end of an arm
in the middle of an arm
items.e: The centre goes on the vertex, where the two arms meet. Then line up one arm with 0.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the right, so read the inner scale. It counts counterclockwise from 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 135. The small marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 130 and 140 is 135. The outer scale says 45 there, but it counts from the other side. The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 135° makes sense.

items.q: Wei wanted to draw an angle of 70°. His base arm is on 0 of the outer scale. The picture shows what he drew. What angle did he actually draw?
items.e: The base arm is on 0 of the outer scale, so read the outer scale: the second arm is at 110, so the angle is 110°. Wei used 70 on the inner scale by mistake. 180° − 70° = 110°.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the right, so read the inner scale. It counts counterclockwise from 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 110. The outer scale says 70 there, but it counts from the other side. The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 110° makes sense.

items.q: One arm of an angle is on 0 of the outer scale. Which scale should you read?
c: the scale with the smaller number
the scale with the bigger number
items.e: Read the scale that starts at 0 on your arm. Here that is the outer scale.

items.q: Kai wanted to draw an angle of 50°. His base arm is on 0 of the inner scale. The picture shows what he drew. What angle did he actually draw?
items.e: Read the inner scale, because the base arm is on its 0: the second arm is at 130, so the angle is 130°. Kai used 50 on the outer scale by mistake. 180° − 50° = 130°.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the right, so read the inner scale. It counts counterclockwise from 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 65. The small marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 60 and 70 is 65. The outer scale says 115 there, but it counts from the other side. The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 65° makes sense.

items.q: Ryan measures an angle that is clearly smaller than a right angle. The arm crosses the protractor at 35 and 145. What is the angle?
items.e: An angle smaller than a right angle is acute, less than 90°, so it is 35°. 145 is on the other scale.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the left, so read the outer scale. It counts clockwise from 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 55. The small marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 50 and 60 is 55. (The inner scale says 125 there.) The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 55° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the left, so read the outer scale. It counts clockwise from 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 145. The small marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 140 and 150 is 145. (The inner scale says 35 there.) The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 145° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 at the right, so read the inner scale. It counts counterclockwise from 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 40. The outer scale says 140 there, but it counts from the other side. The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 40° makes sense.

items.q: Emma measures an angle and writes 40°. The angle is clearly obtuse. What should she have written?
items.e: An obtuse angle is more than 90°. Emma read the wrong scale: the other scale gives 180° − 40° = 140°.

sets.title: Angles on a line and around a point

items.q: The angles make a straight line. What is the missing angle?
items.e: First add the angles you know: 40° + 55° = 95°. Then 180° − 95° = 85°. (265° comes from using 360°.)
The line is tilted, but it is still straight: 180° − 140° = 40°. (50° is 90° − 40°: the line is not a right angle.)
Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. 180° − 55° = 125°. (305° comes from using 360° instead of 180°.)

items.q: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. Angles around a point add up to …
items.e: Around a point is a full turn: 360°. A straight line is only half a turn: 180°.

items.q: Two angles make a straight line. One angle is 72°. What is the other angle?
items.e: 180° − 72° = 108°. Check: 108° + 72° = 180°. (112° comes from a subtraction slip, 18° from 90° − 72° and 288° from 360° − 72°.)

items.q: Two angles make a straight line. One angle is 4 times as big as the other. How big is the smaller angle?
items.e: The smaller angle is 1 part and the bigger one is 4 parts: 5 parts make 180°. 180° ÷ 5 = 36°. The bigger angle is 4 × 36° = 144°. (45° comes from 180° ÷ 4, and 72° from 360° ÷ 5.)

items.q: The angles make a straight line. What is the missing angle?
items.e: The small square is a right angle: 90°. 90° + 62° = 152°, and 180° − 152° = 28°. (118° comes from 180° − 62°, forgetting the right angle.)

items.q: Two angles make a straight line. One of them is obtuse. How do you classify the other one?
items.e: The two angles add up to 180°. The obtuse one is more than 90°, so less than 90° is left: the other one is acute. (For example, 120° + 60° = 180°.)
The six equal angles add up to 360°. 360° ÷ 6 = 60°. (30° comes from 180° ÷ 6.)

items.q: The angles make a straight line. What is the missing angle?

items.e: Angles around a point add up to 360°. 360° − 110° = 250°, a reflex angle. (70° comes from using 180° instead of 360°.)

items.q: The angles make a straight line. What is the missing angle?
items.e: The small square shows a right angle, 90°. 180° − 90° = 90°, so the other angle is a right angle too.
180° − 35° = 145°. (55° is 90° − 35°: the line is not a right angle.)

items.q: Three angles go around a point: 100°, 120° and 140°. Olivia says they are correct because they add up to 180°. What is wrong?
c: One angle must be a right angle
items.e: 100° + 120° + 140° = 360°. Angles around a point make a full turn, so 360° is correct. 180° is for angles on a straight line.
360° − 80° = 280° is left for the two equal angles. 280° ÷ 2 = 140°. (50° comes from using 180°: (180° − 80°) ÷ 2.)
Add the angles you know: 100° + 130° = 230°. Angles around a point add up to 360°: 360° − 230° = 130°. (260° comes from subtracting only 100°.)

items.q: Three angles go around a point. Two of them are 90° and 120°. What is the third angle?
items.e: 90° + 120° = 210°. 360° − 210° = 150°. (210° is the sum of the two angles, not the missing one, and 60° comes from 180° − 120°.)

items.q: Four equal angles go all the way around a point. How big is each one?
items.e: 360° ÷ 4 = 90°. Each one is a right angle. (45° comes from 180° ÷ 4.)
Add the three angles you know: 70° + 80° + 95° = 245°. 360° − 245° = 115°. (185° comes from forgetting the 70° angle.)

items.q: What is the size of the marked angle between the hands at 4 o’clock?
items.e: The 12 spaces between the numbers go around a full turn, 360°, so each space is 360° ÷ 12 = 30°. At 4 o’clock the hands are 4 spaces apart: 4 × 30° = 120°.

items.q: In a circle graph of favourite sports, the section for soccer makes an angle of 120° at the centre. What fraction of the circle is it?
items.e: 120° out of 360°: 360° ÷ 120° = 3, so it is one third. (One half would be 180°, and one quarter 90°.)

items.q: In a circle graph of favourite sports, the section for hockey is one quarter of the circle. What angle does it make at the centre?
items.e: A full circle is 360°. One quarter of 360° is 360° ÷ 4 = 90°. (25° confuses a quarter with 25%.)

items.q: Soccer practice in Surrey runs from 3:00 p.m. to 3:45 p.m. How many degrees does the minute hand turn?
items.e: 45 minutes is three quarters of an hour, so three quarter turns: 3 × 90° = 270°, a reflex angle. (45° mixes up minutes and degrees.)

items.q: A BC Ferries boat leaves the dock sailing east. It turns 45° counterclockwise. Which way is it sailing now?
items.e: Counterclockwise from east turns toward north. 45° is half of a right angle, so the boat points halfway between east and north: northeast. (Southeast would be 45° clockwise.)
The flat ground is a straight line, so the two angles add up to 180°. 180° − 25° = 155°. (65° is 90° − 25°, and 335° is 360° − 25°.)

items.q: A classroom door is opened so that it makes an angle of 100° with the wall. How do you classify this angle?
items.e: 100° is more than 90° but less than 180°, so it is obtuse.

items.q: A garden sprinkler in Kelowna waters while it turns through 150°. What angle around the sprinkler does it not water?
items.e: The watered angle and the dry angle make a full turn: 360° − 150° = 210°. (30° comes from 180° − 150°.)

items.q: A wind turbine has 3 blades spaced equally around the centre. What is the angle between two blades next to each other?
items.e: The 3 equal angles go all the way around: 360° ÷ 3 = 120°. (60° comes from 180° ÷ 3.)

items.q: On Grouse Mountain, Owen measures the slope of a ski run with a protractor and writes 155°, but the slope is clearly acute. What is the angle?
items.e: An acute angle is less than 90°. Owen read the wrong scale: 180° − 155° = 25°.

items.q: How many degrees does the minute hand turn in 20 minutes?
items.e: The minute hand turns 360° in 60 minutes, so 6° each minute. 20 × 6° = 120°. (240° is the other 40 minutes.)

items.q: In coding class, Ava’s robot faces north and turns 90° clockwise three times. What single counterclockwise turn would get it to the same direction?
items.e: 3 × 90° = 270° clockwise. A clockwise turn and a counterclockwise turn that end in the same place add up to 360°: 360° − 270° = 90° counterclockwise.

items.q: A Ferris wheel has 10 cars spaced equally around its centre. What angle at the centre is between two cars next to each other?
items.e: The 10 equal angles go all the way around: 360° ÷ 10 = 36°. (18° comes from 180° ÷ 10.)

items.q: What is the size of the marked angle between the hands at 10 o’clock?
items.e: From 10 to 12 is 2 hour spaces. Each space is 30°, so 2 × 30° = 60°. (300° is the reflex angle the other way around.)

items.q: A snowboarder at Whistler spins one and a half full turns in the air. How many degrees is that?
items.e: One full turn is 360°, and half a turn is 180°. 360° + 180° = 540°. (450° is 360° + 90°, a turn and a quarter.)

items.q: At a skating club in Kamloops, Jasleen spins two and a half full turns. How many degrees does she turn?
items.e: Two full turns are 2 × 360° = 720°, and half a turn is 180°. 720° + 180° = 900°. (450° comes from using 180° for a full turn.)

items.q: A cedar tree leans after a storm. It makes an angle of 80° with the flat ground on one side. What angle does it make with the ground on the other side?
items.e: The flat ground is a straight line, so the two angles add up to 180°. 180° − 80° = 100°. (10° comes from 90° − 80°.)

items.q: After a hockey game, a round pizza is cut into 8 equal slices from the centre. Mateo’s team eats 3 slices. What angle at the centre do the slices that are left make?
items.e: Each slice is 360° ÷ 8 = 45°. 5 slices are left: 5 × 45° = 225°, a reflex angle. (135° is the 3 slices that were eaten.)

items.q: Arjun hikes a trail in Stanley Park. At a bend, the angle between the two straight parts of the trail is 150°. How many degrees did he turn at the bend?
items.e: Walking straight on would be 180°. The trail bends to 150°, so Arjun turned 180° − 150° = 30°. (150° is the angle between the paths, not the turn.)

items.q: Chloe is kayaking near Nanaimo, facing west. She turns the kayak 90° counterclockwise. Which way is she facing now?
items.e: Counterclockwise goes north → west → south → east. A quarter turn counterclockwise from west is south. North would be 90° clockwise.
